newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria frees FIS leader Madani in dramatic move.
newsitem.headline: Algeria frees FIS leader Madani in dramatic move.

text.p: Algeria on Tuesday freed radical Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) chief Abassi Madani in what diplomats termed a dramatic step but one unlikely to end violence in the North African country.
The military prosecutor's office in Blida, where Madani had been sentenced to 12 years' imprisonment in 1992, said the measure was a "release on parole".
"It's a dramatic move in terms of the government relationship with the opposition and FIS," said a senior diplomat in Algiers.
"But it is not going to stop the violence like the bomb in Baraki yesterday or the massacres. There's no reason to think that Madani can do that now. His time has gone by."
The FIS leadership in exile has long called for the release of its leader and his deputy, Ali Belhadj, as one condition for putting its weight behind efforts to bring peace back to Algeria.
Analysts said it would certainly welcome the release but could be divided over any change in stance while Belhadj remained held.
Martin Stone, head of research at the London-based Control Risks, also said he did not believe the violence would stop.
"The security environment is very complex. The FIS's AIS (Islamic Salvation Army) is only one of six or seven groups and is not going to stop fighting until the FIS is legalised," he said.
"And the GIA has nothing to do with the FIS and it's that group which is doing the urban bombings like that yesterday."
The Armed Islamic Group (GIA), led by Antar Zouabri, 27, is the most ruthless of the groups and is blamed by the authorities for bombing and massacres in which hundreds have died.
On Monday, a bomb in the Algiers suburb of Baraki killed 26 people and wounded more than 80, mainly women and children, Algerian newspapers said on Tuesday. Security forces said 21 died.

After a weekend in which two influential newspapers reported the massacres of 44 people, most with their throats cut, the government newspaper El Moudjahid said security had suddenly worsened with another massacre -- this time 15 civilians -- in Medea overnight on Monday.
Madani, 66, was serving a 12-year jail term imposed in 1992 for threatening state security after a strike and riots preceded Algeria's first multi-party general election planned for June 1991.
In the unrest, at the height of the FIS's domination of city streets in June, he said: "If the army does not withdraw we will be obliged to call a jihad (holy struggle)."

Two days later, he and his hardline deputy were arrested. The election was put off to December 1991. And after the FIS took a huge lead in the ballot, the authorities cancelled the results and a planned second round.
Just months later, in growing violence, Madani and Belhadj were tried and sentenced by Blida military court.

Last week Abdelkader Hachani, the man who led the FIS in the elections, walked free from jail after being given a five year sentence, covered by his period in detention. The prosecutor asked for 10 years on charges of trying to undermine state security.
The influential El Watan newspaper said that light sentence was the first signal that President Liamine Zeroual's government was moving to forge a broad consensus with the opposition.
"If this is confirmed, the authorities will lift the state of emergency...," it said last week.
Legal opposition groups have long demanded that the state of emergency be lifted to enable full political activity in the country of 29 million people.

It was imposed in 1992 during the street unrest and battles around mosques from which the FIS had built its influence. The authorities gradually reimposed control and hardline guerrillas took to the bush.
Security analysts have long puzzled over what if any link exists between the FIS, its AIS wing, the GIA and other groups.
Most say they believe Madani has little sway with the armed groups. His release would have more impact on the legal opposition which wanted to find consensus and reconciliation.

"I would interpret his release as a signal that the government is more than ever confident of its position after its (constitutional) referendum, the presidential election and last month's general election," said one foreign analyst.

Another European source in Algiers said: "This step will be welcomed by many people here and overseas, but not by everybody. Some are already seeing Islamists 'getting in by the back door' through the last elections."
Seven members of an Islamist-leaning party have posts in the government since the June 5 ballot.
Another diplomat, referring to divisions in Algeria between hardliners who believe only force can end an Islamist threat, and those who believe negotiations could bring peace, said:
"It (the release) is not all that surprising but it could be a bit disturbing. It could unbalance things."
